title: Eyes and ears
note: Eye: ophthalm/o or ocul/o (eye), opt/o (vision), blephar/o (eyelid), kerat/o (cornea), irid/o (iris), retin/o (retina); -opia means vision. Ear: ot/o or aur/i (ear), audi/o or acous/o (hearing), tympan/o or myring/o (eardrum). Note kerat/o: cornea in the eye, horny tissue in the skin.

read.title: Two senses, two vocabularies
text: The eye and the ear each have a Greek and a Latin root. The eye is ophthalm/o or ocul/o; the ear is ot/o or aur/i. A specialist in the eye is an ophthalmologist, and the instrument for looking inside the eye is an ophthalmoscope.

Light enters the eye through the cornea, the clear front window, then passes through the pupil, the opening in the colored iris, and is focused by the cornea and lens onto the retina at the back. The white outer coat is the sclera. Notice that kerat/o means cornea in eye terms, while in skin terms it refers to hard, horny tissue, and scler/o can mean the sclera or simply hardening. Vision terms end in -opia: myopia is nearsightedness, hyperopia farsightedness, and diplopia double vision.

Sound travels down the outer ear canal to the eardrum, the tympanic membrane (tympan/o, myring/o). Three tiny bones, the ossicles, pass the vibration across the middle ear to the cochlea in the inner ear, where it becomes a nerve signal. Hearing roots are audi/o and acous/o, so audiometry measures hearing and presbycusis is hearing loss that comes with age.
